And then in late 2019 I watched my first campaign series of Airships: Conquer The Skies by either the YouTuber Lathland or Stuff+. The game had everything I ever wanted: simply beautiful graphics, grand strategy of fleets, no sweaty and toxic tryhards, creative freedom, and airships and landships. Unluckily my computer at the time could never operate such a game, I was studying in an early college, and I didn’t have a good relationship with my parents to persuade them to buy me a new PC. It took me 5 years, graduating high school, joining the army, and currently getting deployed to Kuwait, just to be able to have the independence and financial strength to get a better computer. Comment:
Man this one brings back a ton of memories. One of my favorites:
My older brother had a friend who had an external hard drive full of pirated/cracked games and we would constantly get groups together to do LAN parties. This was one we frequented a LOT. I’ll never forget this one free for all match. we didn’t see one of our friends for a majority of the match. Slowly over time the match was getting more and more laggy, which was kind of normal for how much stuff was going on, and then all of a sudden the game starts slowing down a LOT. One of us starts dying laughing and tells us to come look. We all go over to his screen,  and just see a massive unending red colored blob jumping towards his systems. turns out buddy who was MIA had found some nice pocket where he was left to his own devices and just quietly did research and upped his pop cap until he capped it out entirely with scouts. Game ended up turning into a PowerPoint slideshow and we thought it was the funniest thing. I vividly remember laughing so hard I started crying. 
Games after that naturally turned into a “who could bring the game to a screaming halt via scouts” competition. 
Miss the hell out of those days, thanks for bringing back some nostalgia. :’)

Author: @imperialus1
Comment:
Not a bad review.  I'd say RTFM but it's nearly 400 pages so I'll try to sum up a few of the things you were stuck on.

Regarding scales.  Your dominion score also affects the number of sacred units you can recruit.  For some nations, like MA Ulm this doesn't matter at all, for other nations like Vanheim you will win or loose based on your bless and how many Vanheres (their sacreds) you can pump out. Most nations like neutral heat.  When it is too hot, or too cold it affects province income, resources, and population growth.  Most units don't care too much about heat or cold unless it gets to either extreme of the scales in which case they suffer fatigue penalties or you are playing a nation with cold blooded troops in which case cold provinces will fuck them right over.  They are also more pronounced on units that have cold or heat power in which case they gain attack and defense in provinces that match their prefered temperature and attack/defense penalties in provinces where the reverse is true.  This leads to some hilarious slap fests between nations like Abyssia and Neiffelheim where they can utterly annihilate each other on the defense but can't attack for shit.  Since there are seasons in the game as well the heat/cold scales mean that in a cold dominion it will stay cold through fall and spring and probably only hit neutral heat in the middle of summer.  In hot dominion the reverse is true.  It actually creates quite a conundrum when attacking a nation like Neifelheim because you do not, under any circumstances want to kick off your offensive in late fall.

Regarding magic scales, if you are in a land with magic scales it will lower the magic resistance of all units in it.  If you have drain scales it increases magic resistance.  From the perspective of the caster magic scales lower the fatigue required to cast spells.  The big thing is research points though.  If for example you are playing one of the Phlegra's then you will be churning out dozens and dozens of cheap slave mages.  They are terrible researchers giving 5RP/turn each.  With 3 points of magic though they are now 8RP/turn which makes them some of the most cost-efficient researchers in the game especially once you factor in their dirt-cheap upkeep since they are slaves and you don't need to pay them.

Luck is a zany one.  The community is split between wether or not Luck 3 is the best scale ever or if you should dump it down to misfortune 3 and use the points somewhere else.  The difference between the two is quite noticeable though.  You'll still get bad events with luck but I'm of the opinion that the good events can, and often will bootstrap you up quite significantly when they do pop.

You're conclusion is spot on though.  I've got just under 600 hours in and I've only played 5 multiplayer games, three of which saw me knocked out before turn 50.  My longest running game is about to enter its 5th month.

Author: @diegoakadisciple8336
Comment:
The random number generator is not biased towards the AI. The AI cheats in pretty much every regard past the regent difficulty, but the RNG is not one of them. One of the problems is that most people don't understand the defensive bonus of the units, on top of the results being randomly calculated. A spearman has a base defense of 2, fortification adds a 25%, base terrain varies but the least is a 10% and going as high as 50% for hills and 100% for mountains. Fortifications can be built on top of those for even greater bonuses.

A spearman on a town build on a hill with walls has 100% (hills + walls) + 25% from fortification, and if that town happens to be across a river, a 25% buff is applied. Suddenly the 2 defense spearman has a minimum of 4 defense and could potentially have 5, which could be enough to give cavalry a run for their money at 6 attack, and to possibly stop an early era swordmen offensive flat on its face

A town that has reached 7 population will also get the innate bonus of 50%, at the tradeoff that walls no longer apply .

The easiest ways to deal with those bonuses is to use overwhelming force. The AI will rarely have more than 3 or 4 defenders even up to emperor difficulty. After artillery had been discovered that is also a great way to pretty much guarantee sucess. By artillery I mean the actual artillery piece, earlier form such as catapults miss too often and cannot cross certain terrain.




I got mixed feelings about civ 4. I have come to accept it and like it a bit, but I was royally pissed at a variety of things. Such as the replacement of advisors with clearly displayed info to stale screens that also failed to display the info they were meant to give, the removal of the right click quick reference to the civilipedia, the removal of the siege pieces to actually act as siege pieces and making them work as kamikazes instead, I generally like the civ 3 aesthetic more as opposed to 4, I find the leaderheads a lot easier to take seriously (Although not all are perfect) than say, pacal in civ 4, or others, the merging of the culture mechanic with city defense, culture implementation over terrain as a whole, making military affairs pretty much an all or nothing endeavor, etc.

The new strength point mechanic meant that suiciding anything against stronger foes will still kill them regardless if it's the counter unit or not. The new kamikaze catapults are exceptional as they are both cheap to produce and can damage multiple foes (at the cost of losing the unit because artillery is literally meant to be used as kamikazes)

I never understood the complaints about doomstacks and never will. Haven't played civ 5 or 6 just get but im sure that one is going to be a major annoyance. You build units, you put them on a stack. What a terrible concept. How im supposed to mobilize 30+ units for war if I can only place 1 for each square? What a bullshit solution for a problem that wasn't really a problem. If you misplayed and let the AI build huge forced, you could 1) march their forces 2) bribe others into war 3) use artillery to weaken the stack. All these are viable solutions and mind you, I prefer civ 3 take on artillery (that is, units that can bombard but have no defensive capacity and can be captured) to the absolute bullshit that is kamikazing artillery support into the enemy.

Civ 4 did some things right, IMO, like the civic system or the unit promotion, but it does have some things that bring the overall experience down for me

Author: @Tryptic214
Comment:
This review reminds me of another review I once read, which called Twelve Angry Men stereotypical and cliché.  And my response is the same in both cases: it only appears to be cliché now because this was the FIRST one and everyone else COPIED it.  The reason the sound effects "sound like stock" is because the sounds from this game DEFINED a generation of stock sound effects.  "The game is simple because it only has 2 resources" but games before TA mainly had 1 resource; it was the very ORIGIN of multiple-resource management/conversion in RTS games.  And how are you going to complain that the BT expansion is bad because it doesn't meet the bar...that was SET by CC being the largest RTS expansion of the decade, unit-wise.

Did you just say "I hate that RTS games have become about stuff like hotkeys"?  Back when this game came out, nobody knew how to play RTS games properly.  We were all noobs.

Total Annihilation is not a good game by today's standards, actually.  And the reasons that it is bad are:

1. Poor unit pathing/targeting
2. Poor AI
3. Untuned pace/lack of balance updates
4. Lack of fancy features (damage types, upgrades, special abilities, rank-ups, etc)

All of which are characteristics of a pioneer game that didn't stand on the shoulders of giants like more recent games do.  But to claim that this game was simple for 1997, I think you're having some nostalgia about the OTHER games of that time period.  While I agree that it's obsolete, your review seems to be in response to some sort of straw-man since I've never heard anyone say that TA is still the best RTS in 2018 (Forged Alliance Forever, on the other hand, could legitimately still compete).  You could say the exact same thing with a more positive tone of voice and it would be fine.

Finally, I just have to make one last comment about simplicity.  I once ordered a K-bot to move next to a nuclear reactor, mere seconds before its body was shattered by an artillery shell aimed at the structure.  The reactor survived long enough for my bombers to destroy the artillery.  You don't get that kind of thing in RTS games TODAY, 20 years later.  Complexity comes in many forms.

Author: @ultris07
Comment:
If you are hearing the same song over and over being repeated you might have the loop feature on which is something that this game actually contained back in that day.

That aside, after listening to this review.
You are both right and wrong.

For one you're trying to apply a modern convenience to a game from the early RTS days, at least the early days of which RTS started booming.

And secondly it's really not as simplistic as you might think You might think it's simplistic because of how the game rewards playing but there's a little more that's going on in the background.

First it is one of if not the first RTS to use fully 3D models, which for 1997 is very impressive.
That said technically the land is also in 3D, Well not explicitly visually shown the 2D maps are actually over 3D topographical segments, So you can have things like small hills while not being able to really see them visually clearly they do exist and there is actual elevation in the game.

Second in 1997 compared to modern day the first instance in any RTS that I am aware of for a percentage based income is revealed here in total annihilation.
Since you have a constant static supply always coming in instead of a static amount that you can gain, such as in command and conquer, where each or truck digging regular gold or brings in about 700 in-game currency.
You have to actually manage how much you are draining from your production so as to stay above the red line.
Again while not too dissimilar from that of command and conquer It also doesn't create the no economy scenario meaning that the AI can still function unlike command and cocker even if the resources technically run out for them, Because most if not a handful of units do produce things like energy or metal depending on the type and managing two types of resources compared to one especially since they don't technically run out while not extremely difficult by any means if you have a decent power and metal flow and something gets destroyed or disrupted or you try doing too much at once you're going to pay with extremely slow production.

Third while it is encouraged that you make enhanced fortifications such as artillery and use those as a steel wall against the enemies it is not necessarily required and in fact that way of playing is not really rewarded, sure you might stop the enemy from getting into your base if you build enough artillery But artillery is not the end all be all, It is just a means to an end just like nukes.

One thing I completely agree on is useless units compared to well useful units, however by talking about fog of war as you have shown to completely disregard in this video you're missing a key component of how the game is supposed to be played, which is done in fact through scouting of course disabling fog of war isn't necessarily a bad way to play but it's not the intended way to play.

Fourth as for music, I think you might have had the looping feature enabled, I have had no issues with the steam release.

Fifth As for side imbalances, I think this is where you failed, due to disabling fog of war, since by extension radars are supposed to be your main way together Intel about enemy positions, which mean s being able to see everything the enemy is doing and taking into account that the enemy will always build a plethora of units, is a good way to distract the players radar system, especially when targeting using the radar.
again this is another core feature that you seem to be overlooking for the concept of simplicity when it's more complex than you think.
Which means that the CORE are equally as viable as the ARM.
As in a side I love how you mentioned the big Bertha for the ARM, but not the fact that the CORE have their own long range artillery.

Sixth you forgot to mention somewhere along the way, That bullets are affected by wind velocity, unlike that of lasers which shoot in a straight line because they're not affected by wind turbulence, bullets do have some sway to them after being fired, Well not hugely noticeable since the game can't accurately render extremely high winds so you won't get any bullets literally flying way off course because of wind, if you shoot something like a long range artillery you might notice that the shots won't always land where they should and sometimes might start vearing after being shot.

Seventh going back to the argument about fog of war this is also where combined arms comes into play in a more effective way because you won't always know what the enemy has or how they're going to attack you usually it's with bombers but sometimes they might surprise you with gun ships which are surprisingly tanky, of course there are generally upgrades to certain units that are better than others while some basic units remain the best throughout the game, So it's always good to have a combined effort of both land and air sometimes even sea.

8th and final point I can make out is your concept of steamrolling the AI.
Well sure definitely if you are playing on skirmish depending on the map and the amount of metal spawn or how much metal storage and energy storage you make yourself spawn with, The AI can be a complete pushover even on the hardest difficulty.
But with how you're talking about the AI and how easy it is to beat I don't think you actually actively play the game on the hardest difficulty, which is surprisingly more difficult than you would think, however also with fog of war turned off the AI becomes less difficult because you can see everything the AI is doing if you happen to fly a plane or you know have the full map revealed over the enemy base.
Which in turn leads to your weakest argument about the game being very easy or something along those lines because you're not taking or showing everything you're showing how you like to play.
Which to be fair is a decent way to play if that's how you enjoy the game but overall really leads to a lack of a good review since you're not talking about the things that the game excels at in this regard.
Well the AI is not complicated by any means or extremely well-versed detectable knowledge.
It can more often than not if you are unprepared for an assault leave you reeling from its attacks, especially since the game is meant to be played with fog of war on so it's harder for you to discern what the enemy has where it has it and how many units the enemy has.

Of course most if not all of these concepts have been done better over the years obviously, and while unit passing does suck I still think what the game does and how it achieves doing what it does is really good, especially from a game from 1997, where people initially thought the concept was completely ridiculous and not possible.

And while I don't think the review is bad, It is lacking in many ways. This was a good first attempt but personally I think this "review" needs a "redux".

Author: @D64NZ
Comment:
Micromanagement isn't a strategy, it's just tedious. TA was all about the macro management. So far few games have come close to matching it. I've played all of the Starcrafts and Warcrafts and I enjoy them, but there is no choice of units. You always have a single path to follow. Let alone building a fleet of resource gatherers is just a necessary waste of time where you should be planning your attacks. It never made sense to keep that mechanic in Starcraft. Units that can't auto-cast their own skills are just agonising to use. There's no need to explore or take and hold ground, you just blob your units and roam out once you think you are strong enough. Or you go to the 1 or 2 other places where there are recourses and attack that. Again that's not strategy. 
It TA it is all about holding ground and making the best use of the terrain. Massed rushes don't work because the wrecked units leave behind wreckage which makes a wall slowing down the units behind it. If you switch off the fog of war, of course, it's easy and you don't get it. It's basically cheating. You can just surround the enemy with the enemy with long-range turrets and sit back. and wait. The Big Bertha, for example, is an iconic unit with its extreme range and high damage, but that is useless if it can't see the target. Your base is where you happen to have buildings at the time, and you can lose a few and still rebuild in time for the next attack. Any base without defences, however, will be quickly overrun. 

Only in recent times have other games even tried to model real ballistics. Need to do fast accurate damage?  Use a laser unit. Want to shoot over a hill or wreckage? Take a ballistic unit. Need to guard against air attacks?  Take an AA unit. Is it hilly? Build Mechs over vehicles. Is there an area of water near where the fighting will be? Build the expensive but high damage sea units. Is the terrain too open? Make your own choke points with dragons Teeth. Want to know where the enemy is? Throw up radar towers around the map, and set up flying scout patrols. Has the enemy brought out a Krogoth? Overload it with cheap light units. Getting too many light units rushes? Build weapons with AOE effect. Want the enemy build tree? Go steal one of their construction bots and convert it to your side. The enemy commander is out of position? Go grab him in a transport aircraft. 

Every RTS is about resource management, but you don't have to micromanage that in TA, unlike just about all other games. They won't even let you queue units to build once you do have enough resource for them in many cases. In TA if you want that big expensive unit you don't have to sit around waiting for your legion of resource gatherers to collect enough. You just start building it and hope you either have enough saved up or accept some nano-stall. You are NEVER sitting around waiting for the counter to tick over. It's even worth building a few resource storage facilities just for those big projects, so you aren't wasting the resource you have coming in, and can suddenly drop a big build order. 

That happens a lot since you have real counter play, and using the same approach over and over again means failure. You like using planes? Well too bad cause they just built 20 AA towers and a few flak cannons. So you change and adapt. They are static so you jam their radar and use your own to spot them and use some long-range missiles to take them out. Or do 1 or 100 other things you can do to unpick their defences. The biggest issue it was that there are too many choices, which they fixed to some degree with Planetary Annihilation. You don't get swamped with the entire build tree all at once, and even late game you make choices over the type of units you want to field. I noticed in your video you were only using T1 units, and only a couple of times had some T2 or T3 units. It can be overwhelming to those new to the game, so Planetary Annihilation is probably the best place to start.

Author: @DevinNovelle
Comment:
Veteran DSvania player here. Right before the attack animation ends, press 'LB + D-pad down' to backdash cancel. This will cancel the attack animation, and if you time it right, you can repeatedly do this to kill enemies and bosses much faster.

Extra tip - Tech jumps: When you unlock double jump: While moving forward > Double jump quickly > down-right d-pad + jump to do a "diagonal kick" > double jump quickly > "diagonal kick" > double jump > diagonal kick. This works in all 3 games, and when I played multiplayer for Harmony of Despair, I was always one of the fastest characters, so I know how effective it truly is. You do this technique with winged boots or black panther ability, and you will be even faster.

These 2 tips are crucial for speed, mobility, and damage.

Author: @andywlasniewski6810
Comment: I find the puzzle in Wingspan is to find out how to generate points in every turn. Food isn't (usually) worth points, but can I generate eggs, or tuck cards, or cache food while I'm getting it? There are a finite number of turns in the game, so how can I accomplish as much as possible with each turn? If you play a turn to just get food, or just lay eggs, or just gain cards it does seem boring. And yes, you don't always get the cards you need, but adapting to what's available is the main part of the game. The European Expansion helps a ton with variety and depth. Wingspan was my family's gateway game because we are birdwatchers. It has led us into the hobby from a place of obliviousness, and if that's all it accomplished it would be a great game.

If your side mirrors are properly placed along with your rear view mirror the instant a car comes out of view from your rear view it will be in your side view mirrors effectively eliminating blind spots. Most people have their side view mirrors angled far to much inside towards the side of the car. You can look up videos from professional drivers that showcase the proper angle for side mirrors on your vehicle.

Comment:
What a hidden gem this game is!. I didn't know about it until a good friend of mine suggested we try it. It mixes elements of all the biggies, Minecraft, Stardew Valley and Terraria in particular. I won't spoil it, but do look out for the obvious name drops in the game!. 

However I feel Core Keeper doesn't 'rip off' these games, instead it tries to be different, it merges elements from these games without going full copycat, this is what makes it so good. 

I also like how it doesn't go too much into the lore, which is good for players who like to role play and create their own arcs. 

The 8bit graphics were what caught my eye when my friend sent me the link, because I am a veteran Minecrafter, Stardew player and I have played Terraria many times. 

All in all I would give it 10/10 due simply to the fact there are no game breaking bugs, none that we have come across yet anyway.

There is so much that isn’t touched upon in this review.

Author: @nicocchi
Comment:
This game is really good and is a step in the right direction in making platform fighters a legitimate genre beyond "hurr durr smash ripoff". Even without Workshop support, the game is a must-buy for Smash players that care about the gameplay itself (especially, but not limited to those that like Melee gameplay) instead of just a collection of Nintendo characters, but don't go in expecting a truckload of fun in single player, there's just not much to do beyond Abyss (a wave-based mode that presents you with challenges such as "multi-man smash", platforming, attacking certain stuff, fighting a boss, etc.)

The game only has 12 characters, but each are really deep. Like, you might consider a character like Shulk, Hero, Robin, or the newly announced Steve to be complex and gimmicky characters in Smash, but even they are very basic compared to what EACH Rivals character has to offer. Even the slow and heavy characters have rewarding options that let them be viable against the more nimble guys, who usually dominate a game like this, and thanks to the complexity and bountiful amount of options each character has to offer, it's a lot harder to find two players of the same character to share a similar playstyle.


Lastly, the gameplay itself isn't a complete copypaste of Smash mechanics. Like a comment below mentioned, there's no shields, no ledge, so it leads to a hectic, hyper-aggressive game with thrilling and rewarding combos. There's an excellent tutorial mode which will explain and task you with doing everything from how to perform jabs, tilts, to walljumps to wavedashes. It even has character-specific tutorials, which will teach you the specific quirks and mechanics of every character, such as Zetterburn being able to burn their opponents to cause damage over time, and getting increased knockback when using a Smash attack on a burning opponent—and Zetterburn is the most straightforward one of the bunch!

That said, if you can, definitely get it on PC for workshop support (which turns it into basically a platform fighter MUGEN) and not having to pay for the online or needing an adapter for your ethernet cable. My crappy 2013 laptop runs it flawlessly

Game_Name: GUILTY GEAR XX ACCENT CORE PLUS R
Author: @senatorwilsonphillips8724
Comment:
5:27 I would like to comment on that "rushed endings" part with a suggestion from what I have noticed when playing all the endings as a whole, by focusing on WHEN this game was released:

During the mid 2000s era, Arcsys had lost the rights to Sammy Sega for all the GG characters that didn't appear in GG1 or in the books,or the ability to make more fighting games. This is the reason why GG2 only had the essencial characters (not even naming Dizzy for copyright problems) and changed to a tower-defense / MOBA gameplay.

This game bombed, and hard. Arcsys was moving to Blazblue as the new FG franchise, and the port for ACC into consoles could be the last Guilty Gear game there could be. And so 

The story of Accent Core + was written with the intentions of giving each character closure on their characters, no matter the cost, and usually gives them a new arc as well. Path 1 is the best conclusion for their character, while Path 2 takes more liberties but ends their stories with a more "bittersweet" tone. They were so sure of these endings that unlike in other entries, the Paths for some characters are the same for the other character involved, and not all Paths 1 were meant to happen in the same timeline.

The Paths 1 for Sol,Ky and Dizzy were used for build-up for Overture (because remember, Daisuke paired Ky and Dizzy without build-up, ACC+ was released a year later). That's why their Paths 2 feel so numb, because those would never be continued.

I-No and Testament also had their paths dedicated to explain their absense in Overture, especially as That Man and Raven appear but not the second servant of That Man. Path 1 leaves them out of the game with a chance to return (I-No is labelled as a traitor and is frozen in time,Testament peacefully protects the Grove ) and Path 2 kills them (I-No by screwing with everyone, Testament gets eternal rest).

As for the others, there are many good examples: 

-May learns she's Japanese and either fully accepts the Jellyfish pirates and Johnny as her family, or can leave in search for her family.
-Potemkin and Chipp become legendary protectors of Zepp on their Paths 1, while their Paths 2 is how Chipp TAKES OVER THE GUILD to cleanse it of corruption and Potemkin dies and passes to legend status as a martyr too.
-A.B.A. completes her arc of giving Flamant Nagel a body ,either a completely human one in her Path 1, or the head of a Robo-Ky after capturing Dizzy on their Paths 2, which is still giving him a body.

And the most obvious case of this: Venom. His story revolves around his nightmares with Eddie and what to do with the Guild after the passing of Zato. After a fight with Millia, he decides he should focus on a new enemy, the P.W.A.B., which yeah it works,but it's doesn't feel like the best ending for his arc. This is why this is his PATH 2, while in in his Path 1 HE KILLS MILLIA, has a final fight on his nightmares to overcome his feelings from Zato and disbands the Guild, finally moving on. No matter the cost, it ended his arc perfectly, and even gave him a new one by mentoring Bridget's brother.

Really, the story of this game is so underrated and could skip a lot more about it, but I hope this wall of text was of any interest.

Author: @fluffysheap
Comment:
This was a good game, the graphics were just good enough that playing it isn't painful to look at even today.

Rescuing your family isn't just for the satisfaction of doing it. Your family members are valuable in the score, and they always give you clues to lost cities or Montalban's hideout, which are also very valuable.

The game is completely open world so you don't ever have to do these things, but as time passes, piracy becomes less profitable compared to currying favor with governors and hunting for ancient treasure. Maybe this is how it should be, you are getting older after all, but it kind of stops being Pirates! and becomes Treasure Hunters! 

Biggest complaint about the game is you can't really lose. No matter how badly you are defeated, you never lose anything but time and equipment. Sometimes this is enough of a setback that retirement is the best option, but you can't die, or otherwise get a hard game over.

Great review. I can't believe I missed it when I comment in one of your MB videos before. Youtube recommended me this video.

The depth in MB's gameplay is second to none. I have never seen such smooth and fast gameplay in a fighting game before. FGO on smartphones and Everyday! Today's Menu for the Emiya Family on Nintendo eshop.

That is a shame in my opinion we miss out the source material outside of Japan. Type-Moon is very popular in Japan which makes their license even more expensive. Believe or not but Melty Blood was more popular than Guilty Gear in Japan. The PS2 version of Act Cadenza sold 10 times more than PS2 version of Guilty Gear XX Reload. Actress Again released when portable gaming had taken over Japan and the mobile boom was a thing. The animation in Melty Blood is what made the game so popular in Japan.

I just happened to be recommended with Tougeki sbo 2006 finals for Melty Blood Act Cadenza
https://youtu.be/WRgCvuDas44

It was the year before Capcom debuted Monster Hunter Festa and become a competitive thing because MH Portable blew up big on PSP. I think the last legs of arcade in Japan was between 2007 and 2010.

The gameplay looks crazy when a pro plays it. Tales of the Ils knew what they were doing to get the audience on their side. What a show off. Hype!

Author: @zonesquestiloveunderworld
Comment:
This game is exceptional, particularly for an indie title - it's essentially indistinguishable from a triple-A title - but I have to say I find it quite mentally taxing to play; I can only handle it in half-hour bursts, punctuated by a stress-free interlude with a visual novel, a point-and-click adventure-puzzler or a low-stakes open world craftathon. 
This was most pronounced in the second and third levels (called _tapes_ in-game), wherein you're relentlessly pursued by a basically invulnerable "boss" while also trying to figure out where to go next, what items you'll need to track down and what to _do_ with them once you get to where you need to go; the bosses can be temporarily deterred but doing so requires wasting finite reserves of ammunition. I found this very frustrating and inspired thoughts of abandoning the game altogether, but fortunately I persisted.

Admittedly I _do_ have similar issues with some other games, so it's probably somewhat endemic to my warped brain, but I found my difficulties with this game particularly disheartening; I _highly_ recommend consulting the impressively comprehensive Neoseeker-hosted walkthrough if you're as easily frustrated as I am, especially when it comes to finding the upgrade items (which somehow continually eluded me despite my habitually thorough exploration). 
However, this is far from a negative, and I grew to appreciate these feelings as an integral part of the game's intended experience. Stress can actually be invigorating in the right context, and frustration can foster open-minded and creative thinking when it's not perceived as insurmountable.

Basically, don't go in expecting a mindless psychological horror shooting gallery - psychological _adventure_ is a far more apt description - and be prepared to scour each level from top to bottom, pay close attention to every note or document you come across, and closely observe your surroundings for clues and abundant environmental storytelling. 

"In Sound Mind" is an absolutely essential game for fellow adventure-addicts, and for anyone who loves a well-written and well-told narrative, and don't let the gunplay dissuade you - it's minimal, not at all gory or ghastly, often almost entirely avoidable and even when it isn't, it's on the low end of the difficulty spectrum and you'll never find yourself starving for bullets. It's true that those horror purists chasing the fear factor won't find satisfaction for that particular itch here; nonetheless I'd still suggest giving it a go, because there's something special about this game. 

The voice acting is phenomenal, particularly that of the protagonist's patients (he's a psychologist) whose minds serve as the game's compellingly diverse levels, each reflecting their individual mental complexes and challenges. The sound design is equally brilliant, and the music, while not stunningly unique, serves its purpose adequately. The graphics are exceptional considering the low budget, and the overall visual design is pleasingly consistent, and while it's generally grounded in mundane reality it offers several idiosyncrasies in the form of the game's enemies and each level's respective "boss". 

The gameplay won't shatter your preconceptions and the gunplay could be called somewhat "generic", but it's a solid, bug-free experience and surprisingly lengthy for an indie title, and _being_ an indie title it's also not too wallet-draining and offers supreme bang-for-your-buck. 

Overall, I'd give "In Sound Mind" an 8/10. It's easily one of the finest indie games ever conceived and I profusely congratulate the programmers, writers artists, designers and actors for their incredible accomplishment - I'll definitely be keeping a close eye on any future releases from this studio!

Author: @shanky.y
Comment:
*Why EURO TRUCK SIMULATOR 2 Stands the Test of Time*

Why does *Euro Truck Simulator 2* (ETS2) continue to thrive, and why will it likely never fade away? Because this game represents the essence of what gaming is truly about. It's a complete, timeless experience that stands apart from many modern titles.  

In the past, gaming was simple: you’d buy a game, own it forever, and play it whenever and however you wanted. Games were finite and fulfilling. Today, that model feels lost. Many modern games are designed to be never-ending grinds, encouraging players to sink years into content they might never complete. Worse, they often include relentless monetization schemes—microtransactions, battle passes, pay-to-win mechanics, and more—that make gaming feel more like a second job than a source of fun.  

Back then, games were the goal, and money was the means to enjoy them. Now, games have become the means for companies to extract money from players. Slowly, this approach has become normalized, with people spending more on virtual items they don’t even truly own.  

This is where *Euro Truck Simulator 2* shines. It’s a game that offers a complete, self-contained experience. You buy it once, and you’re free to enjoy endless hours of relaxing, rewarding gameplay. It doesn’t pressure you with:  
- Season Passes  
- Daily Logins  
- Battle Passes  
- Pay-to-Win Mechanics  
- Loot Boxes  
- Gacha Systems  
- Artificial Difficulty  
- Content Vaulting  
- Membership Plans, and countless other tactics.  

Sure, ETS2 has DLCs, but these are reasonable—new maps to expand the world for those who want them. Considering the game has been running strong for over a decade, this is understandable. The base game, however, is 100% complete, fully playable, and doesn’t require additional purchases to be enjoyable.  

Unlike many modern games, ETS2 isn’t released in a broken state or gutted to sell pieces back to you later as DLC. It’s not a live-service title that collapses when its player base diminishes. It doesn’t demand you reorganize your life around it, or turn gaming into a chore. It’s simply a game—a beautifully crafted game—made for the sheer joy of gaming.  

*Euro Truck Simulator 2* is a rare gem in today’s industry: a title designed to be enjoyed at your pace, on your terms, with no strings attached. It’s proof that games can still just *be games.* And that’s why ETS2 remains perfect.

Comment: You missed a *lot* of this game by basically blowing off the dungeon crawling. Yes, the dungeon combat and enemies do seem simplistic, but you didn't mention (or perhaps even discover) how the decor of your store attracts different types of people, adventurers in particular.  Different adventures do better in different dungeons, for example, and you may never encounter some of them if you don't vary the store's decor. You can also help ensure that your adventurers are better equipped (and increase you merchant rating) by selling them better gear at reduced prices. You also (apparently) missed the finer detail of getting to know your customers, so you can better gauge how much they'll buy and sell for, which (in turn) will help your merchant rating improve more rapidly. Each character who visits your store is different. Although it does seem quite simplistic at first, this game is more than a little bit deeper than you made it out to be. Finally, you didn't mention (or discover?) the game's 3 different modes of play. This game is almost 15 years old now (it was released in 2010), and it deserves better treatment than you gave it, IMHO.

This is definitely one of the best video games I’ve ever played for a remake. Open world Kamurocho is VERY lively and vibrant, plenty of interactions and humorous, creepily intriguing, and heart-warming substories, actually fun and challenging minigames, and the story itself is just as intriguing as anything else. Majima is probably one of my favorite characters in the game; So irritating but you can’t help but love to interact with him due to his VERY random pop ups. The only annoying and repetitive thing I found about the game is how often you encounter random fights on the streets from thugs, yakuza and gangsters that literally chase you down when you’re trying to get somewhere. Luckily you can avoid them and run away until they leave you alone but that’s pretty tedious sometimes.

One of the BEST parts about nearly EVERY Dragon Quest game (especially XI!) is that the pacing is so excellent, that you will rarely find yourself having to stop in the middle of a session. The moment-to-moment exploration and story progression is so perfectly in sync, that if you only have an hour or so to play games each day, Dragon Quest remains as one of the best possible game series. 

Seriously, it’s the perfect pick-up-and-play RPG. This game feels perfect for long sessions and incredibly short ones too, which actually has contributed to its staying power in Japan. Older generations that are perpetually busy find themselves playing Dragon Quest before bed, and younger generations get to experience the games in as much free time as they have. So if you’re a kid or an adult, this series is made for you. It will never disrespect your time. And for that reason, it’s one of my favorite series of games ever.

Author: @Fetablue
Comment:
I think BF4 is the best game of its kind, but it has too many faults. When trying to make real things arcade-ish, you have to completely change up the formula. With the overwhelming amount of content, BF4 is extremely unbalanced and there are too many parts of the game that have no best solution to fixing this problem without recreating the game from the ground up.
BF4 does not adhere to every play style and experiences differ between computers and servers. Vehicles overpower infantry in almost every map and the infantry combat is killed by the terrible tick-rate (netcode) that is as such as to lower the requirements of the game to sell to more people.
The play style I like in FPS games is a high focus on strategy, positions, and communication. But with the game's high health and movement speed, the game becomes a terrible blend of a tactical and a twitch shooter. This is one of the reasons as to why the snipers are so controversial; those who play slowly and safely with communication can overthrow a sniper from his position while those who run and gun get frustrated when shot since they couldn't locate the sniper or even know that there was one in the first place.
I use to love the game, but the problems are unexpected and made the game almost completely unplayable. The moment I bought Insurgency I threw BF4 out the window.
And that is my honest opinion about BF4. Feel free to correct, but think before you do so.

Comment:
I have gone through all of the Slugcats added in Downpour and I can thoroughly recommend it if you enjoyed the base game. 

It's a lot more story focused and consistently more difficult than the Survivor. There are some twists in there that are really fucking cool, and of course the gameplay with the new slugcats is very fun. Also, the co-op works pretty good, but the camera movement issue is even worse with it. There's a mod in the workshop that is an absolute lifesaver called SBCameraScroll by SchuhBaum that fixes that by just having the camera move centered on you and I don't think I'll turn that mod off ever, even for single player. The co-op works through Steam Remote Play so only one of you needs to actually own the game to play co-op. This isn't any fault of Rain World specifically, but the connection through Remote Play has always been a bit unreliable for me, but maybe it'll work better for you.  It's also quite unfortunate that you can't play the co-op on the new slugcat's journeys.

I don't think I'll make a full video on Downpour, so consider this my review. If you like Rain World but thought it was a bit too difficult on Survivor, maybe it's not for you unless you're only interested in the co-op. If you wanted more story that was a bit more understandable and accessible, you can find some of that here (but there's still plenty of incomprehensible spiritual & existential stuff in here as well). If you want some new stuff to shake things up: all the new slugcats play quite a bit differently to the base game ones, there's plenty of new horrible predators, and it doubles the game's region count. I highly recommend it, this is now one of my favorite games ever.

Edit: Well, I ended up making a review on Downpour. Go watch it for my full thoughts on the expansion.

Author: @gammaboy4568
Comment:
23:21 This is no longer the case as of the Remix update, released alongside Downpour. Key items will now respawn when lost permanently-- including to scavengers, which can be exploited to gain quick reputation. It will attempt to respawn the item in the room is was last seen in when the cycle continues. If left behind, for instance, they should appear near where they were dropped in the same room. However, I do believe that scavengers can move the pearl to a different location. It should respawn in the initial position you found it in if it is stored by them or otherwise unable to be recovered.

If this is NOT behaving as expected, you may want to check your remix settings. "Key item tracking" should be enabled by default, but it may be disabled manually. The Classic preset does not disable this option, as it is more of a preventative measure against softlocks or gating features as an undesired punishment. This is the setting which was added to address the concerns of lost key items, as the items included are more important as of the DLC. This feature applies to Hunter's key items, various story-relevant objects in DLC campaigns, and of course all Colored Pearls. "Key items on Passage" is a separate setting, which may be useful to some who find transporting the colored pearls unnecessarily tedious.

Further note, if you are interested in uncovering the lore there is a bonus "Collection" feature included in the DLC. With More Slugcats enabled, any pearls you have read will be kept there along with some other text-based collectibles. For the few that like 100% completion, this adds a neat sense of progress to an otherwise purely extrinsic experience.

Author: @DrJStrange
Comment:
I've got to disagree with the comment about the story being thin. While, yes, the base story itself is quite thin, it feels a lot more metaphorical than that. Oh yeah, spoiler warning, I'm spoiling the whole thing here.




Each society has their own representation of a god, whether that be literally God, duty, beauty, transformation, or exile, and they all use these as excuses to separate themselves from one another. It's a beautiful story about how cultures use their alleged differences to separate themselves and refuse to understand eachother (in the game's case, literally, since they speak different languages), yet the thing they all seek is the same thing: connection (since the glyphic representations of the 5 societies' gods are all the same symbol in different rotations).

I think the game tries to tell the player that forming connections, especially with people you don't know and don't fully understand, is the most important thing that we can do. Just because somebody seems different: has a different culture with a different language in a different script with different histories, doesn't mean you can't learn to understand eachother. It just means you need that communication.

This is pushed further when looking at the primary antagonist, Exile itself. Exile is, realistically, the one keeping everyone separated, most literally shown with the final culture, the fairies, by keeping them locked in a virtual reality. The fairies themselves are also the catalyst of communication, since they built the tower. Less obviously:
- The alchemists' desire for transformation, for ascension, stops them from connecting with the lower levels
- The bards' desire for beauty, their obsession with themselves and their egos over the warriors, have made them unbothered to connect
- The warriors' obsession with duty, their cyclic busywork of moving boxes around, has made them antagonistic to the devotees
- The devotees' worshipping of God, their need to ascend, renders them incapable of connecting with anyone along the way.
In the end, in their pursuit of their culture's philosophy, they all reject connection, the very thing their philosophy's glyph represents. Exile is especially clear here: despite being yet another incarnation of connection, it only serves to divide people

This is a bit more speculatory, but I also think Exile (and the tower as a whole) represents the internet and, more specifically, the way its used. It was built to be a hub of connection and communication, but has since been used to either divide people into factions incapable of intercommunicating, or isolating people entirely. It's completely severed the fairies from other cultures and eachother, and in doing so has made the other cultures unable to communicate. The devotees hate the warriors for closing the door, the warriors consider themselves lesser than the bards and dare not enter, the bards are too scared of the monster to meet the alchemist, the alchemists are too scared of the monster to meet the fairies, the cycle repeats.

Author: @xdearlifex
Comment:
I loved this game. It's important to note that the game regularly confirms in batches of three if you're right about someone's fate. If you get three right, the game will tell you exactly which fates. Its kinda cheesy, but i used this mechanic to figure out several fates in the latter half of the game. 

There is one dude who plays a pivotal role in several scenes, but is never shown doing the job he has. He's shown in the crew sketches standing next to people involved in his job, but you don't know how significant that is at first since you'll often see people mingling in those pictures. The only way I figured him out is by inputting random names while knowing I had 2 other fates correct, so I knew the second I picked the correct name the game would confirm it. It kinda felt like cheating, but I did this multiple times, especially with the Chinese topmen who have very little dialogue. 

Also, I didn't take any notes while playing. I found everything easy to follow since if you select someone in your book you can get a map of the ship with every scene they're in clearly marked with arrows pointing out the order. This is especially useful for disappearances during the beast chapter.

Author: @360Fov
Comment: Unexpected top quality game, your characters age, they grow, and have stories of their own. They can die, too. They fall in love, they have kids, they chase dreams and make terrible decisions... It’s those subplots, and the chaotic and enjoyable battles that make your characters unusually meaningful, rather than just numbers. It's recommended to play this game with a controller, as the mouse can take some of the gritty crime-thriller drama away from the game. The storyline isn't like Game of Thrones despite the use of satirical analogues to the main stars of Thrones. The game is about legacy and books, stories and people, the characters know they're not real, which adds to the realism of the fantasy immersion. Not to be played alone though, it gets quite complicated and you will need emotional support if your characters are injured, maimed, homeless or overly flirtacious. Its possible for your characters to have kids, but impossible for them to have kids with each other. Its up to the player to realize the only route to reproduction, which explains the Blue Chew sponsored 24 hour livestream of Wildermyth taking place at launch weekend.

Author: @Tdrgv512
Comment:
This review felt half-assed and I find it lacking other aspects of the game that are important. I'm sorry, but I can't let it slide. 
Could've mentioned how fast and visceral races can get, Ai are absolutely ruthless in this game as if you're racing against another person. It can also get insanely intense when races get interrupted by other racers or team members of the same team trying to take you down.

It can be terrifying due to your WATER TEMP. And OIL TEMP continuously rising as these rivals constantly coming at you wanting to take you out. Because the higher those temps get, the more your car stresses and slow your car down breaking your flow. Absolutely intense races I haven't had IN AWHILE. Your muscles tense and a huge sigh of relief after it all.

Think of it like fighting a dark souls boss as they have different phases. I'm not saying this is the same thing, but it's got a similar feeling to that.

Another thing wasn't mentioned was the water and oil temp. Temp rises if you keep racing intensely, but can be cooled back down when driving slowly, parked on the road and take a break, or go to one of the pit areas. A mechanic which you have the option to turn off, however you'll get more rewarded if you have it turned ON. And in Pit Areas, you can also call a mechanic to improve the performance of your car, tweak your car settings, refill your nitrous and new tires so you can get back on the road.

As a fan of the series, I appreciate the review, but it's very lacking and you didn't show many cars being driven as if you didn't finish the game.

Author: @SquirrelNuggets
Comment:
They need investors. I’ve been following the games development since I first heard about it when I was in 9th-10th grade, almost 15 years ago. The development has been very slow with very little marketing so I forgot about it for years, and recently purchased it on Steam a few months ago. While it’s been fun building cars and driving them in BeamNG, brilliant feature to have, and it’s insane some of the designs the community has been able to come up with, it’s almost all achieved with mods. They advertise it as a tycoon game but the sandbox mode is what sells it. There’s quite a few features that players have been requesting, certain engine configurations for example, but the dev team doesn’t deem them financially viable because they’re uncommon in the real world. In a game where people are encouraged to express their creativity, that kinda seems like a huge miss. I understand development costs and time management, the game is still in early access after all, which is why I think they need crowd funding. A $30 price tag can only go so far when you don’t have good marketing and Steam takes almost half of that. 14 year old me was enamored with this games concept and I do enjoy it as it’s been a huge consumer of my free time, but I don’t feel like it’s current state justifies its development time. Correct me if I’m wrong but I’m pretty sure as of January 2025, they’re in active development of a track builder…for a game where you’re not actually driving…that time and money can be spent improving the actual game itself and finally get it out of early access.

Sorry for the essay. Those are my thoughts. I love the game but I think the small dev team bit off way more than they can chew and could benefit from funding and oversight.

Author: @Boomerkbom57
Comment:
In case you're curious about the whole "Furry weeb thing with hardcore gameplay" I can assure you that the target audience is not nearly as far away as you'd expect. Bullet hell games in general are largely dominated by people who are all for the aesthetic. While there are definitely people who focus on clicking through visual novels, there are also tons of them playing very hardcore games, just that most of them, like rabbit and steel, have visual styles that most people outside of those communities don't approach. They also aren't approached as much due to their difficulty. The Lunar mode in Rabbit and Steel (The highest difficulty) is often the default in many of the bullet hell games these people play.

There's actually a reason why there are so many incredibly hard bullet hell games with this aesthetic is because most of them are inspired by one franchise: Touhou. It is filled with a massive line of anime girls that look exactly how you'd expect them to look, but if you look at the gameplay the difficulty these games reach are insane. The Touhou games have lead to a massive series of games along with many games being inspired by them, such as rabbit and steel, most of them adopting the same aesthetic.

You can see similar levels of insane difficulty in rhythm games. Looking at the charts in games like Osu you can see inputs requiring insane speed and precision to pull off. Hate furries and anime all you want, but you gotta respect it at some point, shit's crazy

Author: @Bunkerknacker_Retro-Nostalgie
Comment:
What can I say? The perfect review and so damn spot on, it is a bit creepy.
Turok is still a damn fun game and just listen to that pushing tribal soundtrack while slaughtering savages, shamans, mechs and dinosaurs never gets old. Just played the emu a few weeks back and it still kicks ass like the other classics of that time.

Having watched the release steam by GOG on twitch yesterday, all the aspects mentioned are valid and were part of the interview with the developer alongside. The checkpoint or autosave function was also part of it and I must admit, we really are spoiled today. Also, shooting MORE soldiers to the face with the alien gun, watching them fly through the air by the detonation after the weaker impact, is nothing short of satisfying. Such perfect impact in the literal sense simply never gets old.
I can't await to see how they turn Turk 2 into a game that doesn't suffer from fps drops left and right, they did a perfect job on this one.

However, there is more than just the graphical improvement on the technical side, some sections have significant improvements making them a lot more interesting. For one, they replaced long canyon passages with more interesting things such as ruins, temples and the like and they removed these boring and lenghty passages that were pointless, for instance in the catacombs level. Praise heavens! Then again, the fog really adds to the overall atmosphere and really doesn't feel like a limitation at all. 

Oh, if you should have bought it on GOG and you should crash on falling down long distances, disable the galaxy thingy and launch it directly. The dev mentioned they are aware of it and already uploaded another built without galaxy support, so that should already be fixed.

I agree with the price tag being a bit steep, but then again we saved so much on the bullshit Triple-A we got served this year and the next sale is soon to come as well, so... patience is a virtue.

Author: @rodh1404
Comment:
The game can be really good, in the beginning. You touched on this in the video but there's really not a whole lot of actual interaction going on. Outside of the tutorial and scripted interactions with rivals, there isn't a whole lot of roleplaying in the game. And that hits hard in the end game because as the game progresses and you accumulate money, the grind gets real. You just wait until you can rent or buy another building and open another shop. That's when the lack of other things to do really shows itself. Your headquarters / warehouse(s) and shop employees should make it so that you never have to deal with your already established stores, so it's not unusual for me to have the character sleep/rest for 12 hours straight. After which it's just have a meal and go back to sleep again. It's a game which is in desperate need of making that end game more meaningful. Rivals do add an end game challenge, but once you understand how the game works it's not especially hard to take them down, it's just time consuming.

Another flaw (IMO) is that the best way to play the game is to rent an apartment, but not live in it. You're far better off if you spend your resting time in the two parks the game provides. Likewise, I find that having a car is a huge disappointment. The car handles terribly, and as you've mentioned it gets expensive because it's so easily damaged. I just sell it immediately in the tutorial and mostly use the subway since it's SO much better. You will have to buy big trucks and drive them to your warehouse(s) in the mid and late game, but aside from that I don't drive vehicles at all.

Game_Name: FIVE NIGHTS AT FREDDY'S: HELP WANTED
Author: @kyledavis23
Comment:
In my opinion, this game is the peak of the Five Nights at Freddy's Franchise. This game amazingly took concepts and levels from the older games and put it into an extremely polished "best of" collection. It also fixes my biggest problem with the series up to this point: the scariness. Back when the first game released, everyone thought that was the scariest game ever. But, for me at least, each new installment was less scary than the last. But Help Wanted brought back my fear and love for the series by putting the game into VR. I also love how much more polished this game is to the originals. If I wanted to replay FNAF 2, I would play it though this game vs. the original any day of the week. I also really enjoy how much lore and secrets are put into this game, and the DLC too. It reminds me of those iceberg memes, where you can have a basic understanding of the "surface" level, but never dive deeper into that, and still greatly enjoy this game. You can simply play all the levels and get the bad ending, but most people would be satisfied with that. For me, however, I explored every level of this iceberg, getting every ending, including the DLC.

So TLDR: Play this game. Even if its your first FNAF Game ever, its an amazing place to start.

Author: @yoji-_
Comment:
The reason the music syncs so perfectly is because it uses Wwise. Wwise can essentially link specific events in the game to specific parts of music or tracks and dynamically switch between them immediately. Some of the Total War games also use Wwise and it's why the music there so perfectly flows between ambient idle in battle, to more tense build-up during the first charge into the enemy army, into full on battle music after contact is made. All of that is done entirely unscripted obviously and the sound engine itself handles all of it based on what's actually happening in the game. So, the music changing from scary horror running away music to something more intense and action-like when you turn around to fight the alien is because the sound engine picked up your actions and is suiting it.

I'm sure other audio engines also use this capability in a similar way, but I've personally modded with Wwise and it was really impressive how easy it was to use and how effective it is too.

Author: @xomvoid_akaluchiru_987
Comment:
The controller controls on pc are the same as console controls. I've never had a problem with it, you can play at the same level no matter what platform you use. I personally use the quick select controls for controller, when I play it on console. The PC version has the additional bonus of being able to play the not so unbalanced older versions, having save file modifiers, and being able to be modded (as the admin of the modding server, yeah we're still working on that I promise.)

On the topic of difficulty, each one has a set number of turns, the higher the difficulty the less turns you have to clear islands. There are turns in very hard where you will see 4 islands all on the same turn, it's pretty wild. Obviously hard viking varients come sooner, and there are way more vikings in general. Each difficulty steps up the pace of the game, until, at the end of a very hard campaign, you're frantically using all the abilities and items you have to defend an island without losing any houses.

There are a few aspects of Bad North that players commonly engage in: 
1. The strategy and planning. Whenever you're on the map you're thinking _What upgrades do I get? What island do I go to next? What risks can I take?_
2. Macro management, this is your real time tactics! Small tactics and recognizable patterns that you use to respond to the oncoming threats, this is your usual gameplay.
3. Micro management, this is when you move your commanders around while they are currently in battle to chabge the odds ever so slightly more in your favor. You don't have to micro manage at all in order to beat the game even on Hard mode as long as you do the other parts well.

This is my interpretation of micro and macro management, as well as real time tactics (or RTT) which is a subgenre of RTS.

Okay, so the island generation has issues, and when Oskar tried to fix it meant that houses had less space to spawn, so the amount of coins in each campaign was way too little. To counteract that they added islands with tons of money, but it's implemented in the worst way possible. Eldorado is a word for a "city of gold" and also the name of a very specific kind of island generation. A massive flat island that always has extra enemy types, and is filled to the brim with houses. The issue is that they are flat, boring, and way to difficult. The only "terrain" you have to leverage is the houses around you, and those are really boring. I want to fix this in a mods, but that's a hobby atm and it's taking forever. Flat islands generate naturally without an eldorado as well, and no amount of walls or trees will make them any more interesting. My proposed solution is to remove flat islands from the game, and add bigger island that generate occasionally, along with eldorados that have special tower/multi-leveled buildings that give more money. 

So, pikemen are not the best in the game. In fact they're the worst. Archers don't need high ground, put them on the shore, upgrade them to max, give them any combination of heavy weapons, fleet of foot, and ring of command, and watch as they slaughter all of the shield vikings coming to the island. Archers neutralize threats faster than anything else, and they can immediately be moved to take care of all the surrounding threats very quickly.

I have a whole essay on the game design and balancing of bad north that I've been meaning to make for some time, I might as well publish it this week. The premise is that archers were over powered in the very first version of the game, but the devs, bless their hearts, listened to community feedback. Archers got buff after buff after indirect buff until they were unstoppable as they are in the current version. From the heavy weapons and fleet of foot traits to the removal of the red infantry vikings. And that's skipping a few buffs :D
Archers are the meta, out of all the single class very hard mode challenge runs, archers only was the first one to be completed. Followed by infantry, then pikes, and finally militia. Gaaaahhhhhhh!

sorry I'm done ranting. Great review!

Author: @DRAT311
Comment:
This game is frustrating because it is almost great yet falls flat due to poor design choices.  I wanted this game to be a tower defense game with some first person shooter thrown in for fun.  The designers wanted it to be more a first person shooter with a couple of towers thrown in to help you out.  There are some levels where you get the resources to build lots of towers, but in 95% of the levels I find myself wishing I had more walls and more towers so that I could build all of the cool choke points and mazes my imagination can dream up.  It's like being a kid and trying to play with legos when you only have a handful of blocks.

And in later expansion packs the designers' idea of difficulty seemed to be finding new ways to make your towers even more insignificant, shifting the game even further away from strategy tower defense and more to FPS. 

And survival mode is where this game could have been awesome.  But once again I think the designers have a completely different definition of survival.  They seem to think it just means hardmode.  It's exactly like normal but after the last wave of the round, it starts over and the lumes have double health, meaning the difficulty ramps up quickly. It has a 15 tower limit, but its hard to get to that point because your resources increase slowly while monster difficulty increases quickly.  And the feats of strength get turned on for you automatically, whether you want them or not.  My idea of survival is that you have plenty of resources and its all about coming up with the best maze/tower setup for the level. The waves shouldn't cycle, repeating them same monsters sets in the same numbers.  The waves should grow slightly larger each round, until finally you're overrun by 150 normal lumes on round 133, not 15 super lumes on round 33.

And one final sin:  they disabled alt-F4 and then made it take 10 seconds to ascend through loading menus to exit the game.  So you're out of luck when you want to rage quit because you're on round 8 of Canopy hardmode(5 feats of stength) and your character gets stuck between objects(hapens all the time) and you can't move, and you can't suicide because there's no respawn in hardmode and you'll lose unless you can literally do 20 times more damage than all your towers combined.

The difference between perfect and a cluster F of frustration is just a few bad design choices.

Author: @rocovailo2862
Comment:
So I'm about 6 hours into the game and It's still feeling pretty new and fresh. 
I've JUST unlocked the sword dome and still figuring out which upgrade trees/paths I like. But it's also noticeably a matter of what enemies you are fighting. If I'm forced to choose an upgrade that can better deal with a grounded enemy or a flyer type, I'll probably have to start going down that path or risk getting my dome destroyed that wave.

The gameplay loop, while "simplistic" when you break each part down, I think is to the game's benefit. The movement feels just the right amount of precise but floaty where you might get a resource to tumble over or get snagged if you're not careful. The timer feels like it gives you Juuuuust enough time to get one or if you're lucky, two trips for resources.

Like... you start off slow and peaceful, mining away, nothing too problematic, get an upgrade or two. Fight one or two dudes, go back down. Then by like the third wave tensions start to rise. Mining is a relief after the battle but you're still debating what to go after, where to mine, for how long. Then you debate if you've got time to be greedy or if you should bolt it to the top before the creatures arrive. The fighting isn't super crazy or anything, but it's still good levels of chaotic enough that it really makes for some close call situations. 

I think the game has struck a pretty good balance all in all. It probably won't keep me invested as long as say, a game like Hades. But I don't expect it to.
Definitely has room to grow, but I think this is an amazing game concept I've not seen before and it's style and play is very polished! 
Well worth the $20 imo~

Author: @dropthedice
Comment:
After playing this game and getting a couple endings, I find it hard to be on the same wavelength about the writing. It was by far the worst part of the game for me, making all interactions strain believability to the point of breaking in several instances. This was not the problem with the themes and ideas themselves, which were interesting and very enjoyable, but how they were implemented. In the end I was able to look past the actual writing and focus on the underlying ideas in order to have an enjoyable time.

The gameplay itself is much more easy to recommend, as it's a fairly straight forward management tycoon with a number of randomized events and progression that is gated by the player's knowledge about the game. This is easier to manage since the game will (for the most part) disclose any immediately available progression outlets (i.e. ideas for streams) so it's hard to feel completely stuck at any point in time. The sole exception to this are progression gates that require certain stat levels, which aren't disclosed to the player.

Overall, an enjoyable experience with interesting themes, poor to mediocre writing and engaging gameplay. It doesn't have enough to make someone want to chase all the endings but people can surely get hooked for a good chunk of the game.

It seems kinda pointless to have what's effectively porn, but with the sex cut out.

But because it was made with sex as a central part of the story and experience. In the same way, it's like cutting the action scenes out of an action movie or cutting the scares out of a horror novel. To be fair, SOME visual novels actually benefit from having the sex scenes taken out, e.g. Fate / Stay Night and Kanon. But in those cases, the sex wasn't central to the story (except in the Heaven's Feel route of FSN), and the sex scenes felt crowbarred in to begin with.

Author: @Owlr4ider
Comment:
Warlock 2 on its own is a very solid game, if you ignore all the history. For new players of the franchise who like 4X games Warlock 2 offers a pretty unique 4X experience with the spells(especially terraforming), heroes, plains, etc. However as you said for people coming from Majesty and Warlock 1 it's not much of an improvement. I agree with you that all the DLCs for this game were disappointing. The Naga expansion was a good idea but extremely poorly implemented. It's not even the land vs water aspect as terraforming can turn land into water and vice versa. It's more about the resource allocation, as resources are unique to either land or water so when you switch tiles with resources on them from one to the other the resource is lost permanently removing a very significant layer of the game: getting as many strategic resources inside your regular cities' territory. It's also insanely cheesy as turning large swatches of land into water(with the Lunord specific spell, the regular is just 1 tile per cast) can completely lock out land factions with no access to amphibious units while the opposite(raise land) doesn't have nearly the same impact as the Naga has enough powerful units that suffer no penalties on land. Also the AI absolutely can't handle terraforming to begin, and multiplayer matches get extremely hectic with terraforming all over the place.


With that said, I'm not sure why you decided to make a review on Warlock 2 in 2019 long after it's been released. Not that I mind or anything, but you're still using base pricing which by now is simply irrelevant. Now you can basically get the full game+all DLCs for 75% off. Basically I feel you reviewed this game as if we're still in 2014 rather than 2019 and overemphasized the similarities to Warlock 1 and Majesty whereas most people familiar with those games already knew about Warlock 2 since 2014. Since you reviewed this game in 2019 you should have catered your review to people completely unfamiliar with the title thus de-emphasizing all the reused assets and whatnot and focus on the actual game. If I was a someone who never heard of this game and was considered to buy it this review provided me with 0 information for or against buying it. In fact the 2.5 score might have turned me away if I only looked at the number, but if not I would have found the review completely irrelevant as I had no idea what Warlock 1 and Majesty are so couldn't care less about assets being re-used, lack of innovation, etc. Instead I would have wanted to know how the game plays out, how it fares against other 4X titles, etc, which you provided absolutely no information on.

Author: @vortigauntfan
Comment:
I really enjoyed this game- It's a big time sink but it's really fun if you can get past the fact that there is no other way to win other than just annihilating everyone else. I realized after the first game that I probably wasn't going to win because I always wanted an ally, but this game does get a bit restrictive with trades and there's little chance of ever really becoming liked by another race and getting anything useful from them. There were many times when a trade deal with one species would end and I'd get a message saying that we've come to trust each other more, but when I try to bring back the exact same deal they tell me that I'm either not giving them enough or that they in fact don't trust me enough. 
On top of that, I don't think there's any way at all to convince anyone to have a non-aggression pact or an open borders treaty- they're listed as options but even when I give another species everything they could ever want, max out my reputation with them and set the game on easy negotiation mode they refuse those deals.

Late game gets kind of ridiculous, too, as I constantly found myself getting attacked by the Vulfar and watching their massive fleets of 30-50 warships roll over my forces. Normally it would be nearly impossible to have a fleet of that size because you require expensive command points in order to afford the navy, but somehow other races will end up with 140-300 command points worth of ships while I, after putting as many command points as possible into the game, end up with somewhere around 50.

Aside from stuff like that, though, it's a great game. I still really like playing it because of the combat mechanics. Being able to micromanage the stats of each of your ships from size to speed to whether it's mainly offensive or defensive is really fun, and it's interesting to experiment and test out different setups.

Author: @joelzarley
Comment: This comment probably contains some spoilers, which I guess is appropriate considering the title of the film. I had read the book so knew the subject matter going in. And, while I found the movie incredibly touching (with a few tears), I didn’t find it nearly as gut wrenching as the book (which is a good thing). Obviously, there’s quite a few differences between the two as the story couldn’t be told in exactly the same way, although both are really successful in their respective genres. I think the director made some really smart choices in the translation from book to film. Personally, I really like the sitcom flashbacks since it ties into Michael’s use and love of television as an escape as child, as well as the death scene “interview” since it showed Michael processing Kit’s death in the way where he could best cope with it (by putting on his objective TV reporter hat). I also thought having the camera outside looking in the window (no audio) when Kit told his parents about his diagnosis was really smart and effective. Finally, I think the chemistry between Jim and Ben was fantastic—you have absolutely no trouble believing them as a couple (in all phases of their relationship). The “intimate” scene at the beach house was very well done, and in my opinion really rings true for two people who had been partners for a long time. I’d really been looking forward to this movie and it did not disappoint.

Comment: In my opinion I’m not really that impressed with drunken bat fight.
